note: All people, businesses, phone numbers, account numbers and web addresses in these examples are invented. The checker uses transparent rules, defined in Phase 2, and never says a message is safe.
noSignsText: No common warning signs found. That doesn't prove the message is genuine, so always check payment requests by phone on a number you already have.

low.label: Low concern
low.advice: Probably fine, but check anything that involves money or logins.

medium.label: Medium concern
medium.advice: Don't act on it yet. Check it with the sender using a number or address you already have.

high.label: High concern
high.advice: Treat this as a likely scam. Don't reply, click or pay. Check with the real person or company directly, and report it.

signals.label: Asks to change bank details
signals.explain: It's rare for businesses or staff to change bank accounts. This is the heart of invoice and payroll fraud.
signals.action: Don't pay or update anything until you've called the sender on a number you already have and confirmed the old and new details.

signals.label: Urgency or pressure
signals.explain: Deadlines, threats and 'do it now' are used to stop you thinking or checking with anyone.
signals.action: Slow down. A genuine request can wait the few minutes it takes to check.

signals.label: Sender address looks like one you know, but isn't
signals.explain: Scammers register addresses that differ by a letter or two, swap letters for numbers, or add extra words.
signals.action: Compare the address character by character with one you've used before. Reply to the address you already have, not this one.

signals.label: Unusual payment
signals.explain: Gift cards, cryptocurrency, a new account, an odd amount or a request to keep it quiet are all signs of fraud.
signals.action: Follow your normal payment process, including a second approver. Never pay by gift card or crypto because someone asked.

signals.label: Asks for codes, passwords or remote access
signals.explain: No genuine bank, supplier or IT provider needs you to read out a code, share a password or install remote access because they contacted you.
signals.action: Never share codes or passwords. Only allow remote access if you started the request with a provider you trust.

signals.label: Pretends to be the boss, a colleague or a supplier
signals.explain: Scammers borrow authority and trust. Watch for a familiar name on an unfamiliar address or number, or a request to keep it secret.
signals.action: Contact the real person using details you already have, not the ones in the message.

signals.label: Signs of a fake voice or video
signals.explain: AI can copy a voice or face from a few online clips. A new number, a voice note instead of a call, or 'I can't talk' are warning signs.
signals.action: Hang up and call back on a number you already have. Don't rely on recognising the voice or face.

examples.title: Your password expires today
examples.subject: Action required: your password expires in 2 hours
examples.body:
Dear user,

Your Microsoft 365 password expires in 2 hours. To keep access to your mailbox, verify your account now using the secure link below.

Verify now: http://m365-account-verify.net/login

If you do not verify within 2 hours your mailbox will be suspended and emails may be lost.

Microsoft 365 Support Team
examples.lesson: A login link plus a deadline is the classic phishing pattern. Go to your email account the way you normally do, never through the link.

examples.title: Supplier's new bank details
examples.subject: Updated bank details for this week's payment
examples.body:
Hi there,

Please note our bank details have changed following a move to a new bank. Please use the details below for Friday's payment and all future invoices.

Account name: Harbour Mill Foods Ltd
Sort code: 00-11-22
Account number: 00012345

We need this updated before Friday's payment run to avoid any delay to your next delivery.

Kind regards,
Accounts Team
examples.lesson: Look closely at the address: 'harbourmi11foods' uses the number 1 instead of the letter l. Call the supplier on the number from an old invoice.

examples.title: A quick favour from the director
examples.subject: Are you at your desk?
examples.body:
Hi, are you at your desk? I'm in back-to-back meetings and need a quick favour. I need 6 Amazon gift cards of £200 each for a client thank-you today. Please keep this between us for now, it's a surprise. Buy them and send me the codes by email, I'll sort the expenses later.

Dan
Sent from my phone
examples.lesson: Gift cards, secrecy and a personal email address are a well-known CEO fraud pattern. Ask the real director using the number you already have.

examples.title: Voice note from 'the boss'
examples.body: Hi, it's me, my phone's broken so I'm on this number for now. Listen, I need you to send £4,750 to a new supplier straight away, the account details are in my next message. I can't talk, I'm about to go into a meeting, just get it done before 3 and I'll explain later. Thanks.
examples.lesson: A new number, a voice note instead of a call and 'I can't talk' are classic signs of a fake voice. Call the boss back on the number you already have.

examples.title: IT support needs a code
examples.body: Hi, it's Jordan from your IT support company. We've spotted unusual sign-ins on your business email and need to secure it urgently. You'll get a 6-digit code in a moment, please text it back to me straight away, or install AnyDesk so I can fix it remotely.
examples.lesson: Real IT support never asks you to read out a code. Call your IT provider on its usual number to check.

examples.title: A normal-looking invoice with a twist
examples.subject: Invoice NP-4418 for November
examples.body:
Hi,

Please find attached invoice NP-4418 for November's order, payable within 30 days as usual.

Just to let you know, following our annual audit our account has moved to a new bank, so please use the updated details printed on this invoice going forward.

Many thanks,
Sam Reid
Northfield Packaging
examples.lesson: The address is genuine and there's no rush, which is what makes this convincing. A supplier's real email account can be hacked. A bank change is still a reason to phone.

examples.title: A colleague's new salary account
examples.subject: Bank change before payroll
examples.body:
Hi,

I've switched banks this month, could you update my salary details before payroll runs? New details below.

Account name: P Shah
Sort code: 00-33-44
Account number: 00067890

Thanks so much,
Priya
examples.lesson: Salary diversion fraud looks like a routine request. It comes from a personal address, not the work one. Check with Priya in person or on her known number.

examples.title: A delivery confirmation
examples.subject: Delivery confirmed for Tuesday
examples.body:
Hello,

Your order is confirmed for delivery on Tuesday morning. Invoice HMF-2207 is attached and is payable to our usual account within 30 days.

Any questions, just reply to this email or call the office.

Best wishes,
The Harbour Mill team
examples.lesson: Nothing here matches a common warning sign. That still isn't proof. If an invoice ever asks you to pay somewhere new, phone first.
